extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, meta-analysts, and policy-makers interested in peer review reliability
extracted.subtask_description: A multilevel meta-analysis framework and findings for estimating and explaining inter-rater reliability (IRR) in journal peer review, including methodological choices, covariates to include, and interpretation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability (IRR) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: IRR is defined as 'the extent to which two or more independent reviews of the same scientific document agree.' (Cicchetti)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IRR to quantify agreement among independent reviewers of the same manuscript; relevant coefficients include ICC, Cohen's Kappa, and Pearson r.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ICC when available for measuring IRR
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICC measures inter-rater reliability and inter-rater agreement of single reviewers. An ICC is high if reviewers absolutely agree in their ratings of the same manuscript (absolute consensus) and rate different manuscripts quite differently (consistency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a study reports multiple coefficients for the same sample, include ICCs in the meta-analysis preferentially (the authors included ICCs when available, n=35). If ICC is unavailable, use r or Cohen's Kappa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat about Pearson r and ICC comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Only in the case where ratings by different reviewers have identical means and variances are r and one-way ICC identical. Otherwise, r considerably overestimates the amount of IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To combine ICC and r in a single analysis, transform ICC (square root) to behave like correlation and use Fisher Z-transformations and corresponding standard errors for meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Cohen's Kappa and interpretation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohen’s Kappa was used in many studies; guideline interpretation by Landis and Koch applies (e.g., mean Kappa .17 indicates slight IRR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report Kappa with confidence intervals and interpret using standard interpretive scales (Landis & Koch); be cautious that different coefficients capture different aspects of agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-effects vs random-effects model choice and weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed effects models assume a single true IRR across included studies and weight studies by the inverse of the standard error (so larger-sample studies get more weight). Random effects models estimate the average of a distribution of reliabilities and incorporate both within-study and between-study variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose fixed vs random depending on whether effects are homogeneous; compute standard errors accordingly; use Q test to test homogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multilevel (three-level) models to handle dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Multilevel models allow simultaneous estimation of the overall reliability and between-study variability and do not assume independence of effect sizes. A three-level model (level 1: manuscript, level 2: sample, level 3: study) addresses dependence when a single study reports multiple coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply multilevel models when studies contribute multiple samples/coefficients; this avoids downwardly biased standard errors and accounts for hierarchical data structure (recommended references: Beretvas & Pastor; van Houwelingen et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test and explain heterogeneity using meta-regression
rubrics_metrics.description: When between-study variation (heterogeneity) is high, it is important to look for explanatory covariates using meta-regression rather than relying solely on an overall measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use weighted meta-regression (weights based on study precision), dummy-code categorical covariates, include an 'unknown' category for missing categorical data to retain power, and follow recommendations on minimum numbers of studies for meta-regression (e.g., Baker et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include number of manuscripts (sample size) as a covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of manuscripts (divided by 100 in this study) used to calculate reliability coefficients was used as a covariate because sample size strongly affects the standard error and can reveal publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that studies with larger numbers of manuscripts tend to report smaller IRR coefficients; include sample size to detect publication bias ('file drawer' effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include method of calculation as a covariate (ICC vs r)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-rater reliabilities vary considerably depending on the method used to calculate the reliabilities (ICC or r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for method differences in meta-regression; transform measures (square root ICC, Fisher Z) to make them comparable for pooled analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include scientific discipline as a covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Discipline was coded (economics/law; natural sciences; medical sciences; social sciences) to test whether IRR differs across fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test discipline effects, but be aware the present study found no significant discipline effect — low agreement may reflect lack of consensus at research frontiers across disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include object of appraisal (paper vs abstract) as a covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Object of appraisal (e.g., full paper vs abstract) can affect IRR; abstracts may lead to different reviewer agreement patterns than full papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code object of appraisal in meta-regression; expect abstracts/conference submissions to show different agreement due to abbreviated information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include cohort (time period) as a covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohort (period when manuscripts were submitted) was included to test whether IRR has changed over time (e.g., categorized into decades).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cohort coding to detect temporal trends in IRR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include blinding (single vs double) as a covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Type of blinding (single-blind, double-blind) was tested to see whether masking authors' identities affects reviewer agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for blinding effects, but interpret cautiously — double-blinding can be imperfect since reviewers may identify authors from clues; this study found no significant blinding effect on IRR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include rating system type as a covariate and treat reporting as quality indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating system used by reviewers (metric vs categorical) was included; classification: categorical if nine or fewer categories, metric if more than nine. Mentioning the rating system in the study is itself informative about study quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code rating system and whether it is reported. Expect that (a) more rating scale points can increase reliability, and (b) studies that do not report the rating system tend to report higher (less credible) IRR — non-reporting may indicate lower study quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification rule for rating systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating systems are classified as categorical if they have nine or fewer categories; if more than nine categories, classification is metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this threshold when harmonizing rating scales across studies; consider that increasing the number of rating points can increase measured reliability (Strayhorn et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect publication bias via sample size–IRR relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: A negative association between number of manuscripts and reported IRR indicates publication bias: small-sample studies publish primarily when they report high IRR; large-sample studies publish low IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sample size in meta-regression and interpret significant negative coefficients as evidence of publication bias; adjust interpretation of high IRR findings from small studies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic transformations and estimation details
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the square root of ICC to obtain a correlation-like metric; apply Fisher Z-transformation and corresponding standard errors because correlations are not continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform transformations prior to pooling; use appropriate SE calculations for transformed metrics to compute weights and confidence intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical Bayes (predicted/Bayes estimates) and forest plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Predicted inter-rater reliabilities (empirical Bayes estimates) take into account different sampling errors and shrink small-sample estimates toward the overall mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present forest plots with predicted coefficients and 95% CIs; report and interpret shrinkage effects (smaller-sample studies are shrunken more toward the mean).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software/implementation recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses were performed using SAS PROC MIXED (SAS v9.1.3) and the van Houwelingen/Arends/Stijnen syntax for multilevel meta-analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement multilevel meta-analysis with mixed models (e.g., PROC MIXED) following established syntax examples and references; report software and syntax used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation nuance: high IRR is not always desirable
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much agreement may be a sign that the review process is not working well (reviewers not properly selected for diversity). Conversely, low inter-reviewer agreement may indicate a competent panel representing diverse views and thus may be valuable for validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat IRR magnitude as a sole indicator of quality — consider reviewer selection, complementarity, diversity, and the intended validity goals of the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendations to increase IRR
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence suggests benefits to employing three or four reviewers instead of just two, and a 'reader trial' approach (expert readers per subdiscipline) can substantially increase single-rater reliabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider increasing number of reviewers or using specialized reader systems to raise IRR (examples: reader system produced IRR ~.88 with ~4.3 readers per proposal). Balance increased IRR with potential losses in diversity of perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting completeness as quality criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to report essential study details (e.g., rating system) is an indicator of lower quality and correlates with inflated IRR estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require transparent reporting of methods (rating scales, computation methods, sample sizes, blinding) when evaluating studies of peer-review reliability; treat missing reporting as a covariate or separate quality flag in synthesis.
